summary.text: The continued-fraction recurrence yields \(R_2=U_2/U_3\), where \(U_2=n^2+2n-4\) and \(U_3\equiv2(n-1)(n-3)!\pmod{U_2}\). For \(p\ge19\), quadratic reciprocity makes \(5\) a square modulo \(p\); choosing the larger signed square root \(s\) and setting \(n=s-1\), then writing \(U_2=pc\), gives \(1\le c\le n-3\), so \(c\mid U_3\) while \(p\nmid U_3\), leaving exactly \(p\) after reduction (with \(p=11\) handled directly).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}\qquad(2\le k<n-1),
\]
with
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)-\frac n{-4}=(n-1)+\frac n4.
\]
Thus the continued fraction occurring in the definition of the sequence is
\[
\frac1{R_2(n)}.
\]
If the positive rational number \(R_2(n)\) is written in lowest terms as \(A/B\), then the displayed continued fraction is \(B/A\), and hence \(a(n)=A\). We shall obtain a useful integral numerator-denominator representation of every \(R_k(n)\).

For fixed \(n\ge 3\), define integers \(U_k=U_k(n)\), working downwards from \(k=n\), by
\[
U_n=4,\qquad U_{n-1}=5n-4,
\]
and, for \(2\le k\le n-2\),
\[
U_k=kU_{k+1}-(k+1)U_{k+2}. \tag{1}
\]
The choice of the two terminal values is dictated by
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)+\frac n4=\frac{5n-4}{4}= rac{U_{n-1}}{U_n}.
\]
We will show below that all the relevant \(U_k\) are positive. Assuming that for the moment, downward induction using (1) gives
\[
R_k(n)=\frac{U_k}{U_{k+1}}. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, if \(R_{k+1}=U_{k+1}/U_{k+2}\), then
\[
R_k=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}}
 =k-(k+1)\frac{U_{k+2}}{U_{k+1}}
 =\frac{kU_{k+1}-(k+1)U_{k+2}}{U_{k+1}}
 =\frac{U_k}{U_{k+1}}.
\]

The fundamental invariant of the recurrence is
\[
(k-1)U_k-k(k-2)U_{k+1}=n^2+2n-4 \tag{3}
\]
for every \(2\le k\le n-1\). To prove it, first check \(k=n-1\). Its left side is
\[
(n-2)(5n-4)-(n-1)(n-3)\cdot4=n^2+2n-4.
\]
If the identity holds at \(k+1\), substitute (1) into its left side at \(k\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(k-1)\bigl(kU_{k+1}-(k+1)U_{k+2}\bigr)-k(k-2)U_{k+1}\\
&=kU_{k+1}-(k-1)(k+1)U_{k+2},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is exactly the left side of (3) with \(k+1\) in place of \(k\). Thus downward induction proves (3).

Put
\[
u=n^2+2n-4.
\]
For \(n\ge3\), this is positive. Formula (3), rewritten as
\[
(k-1)U_k=u+k(k-2)U_{k+1}, \tag{4}
\]
also proves positivity of all \(U_k\). Starting with \(U_n=4>0\), descend from \(k=n-1\) to \(k=2\). Since \(k\ge2\), the right side of (4) is positive, and \(k-1>0\), so \(U_k>0\). This justifies all divisions in (2). At \(k=2\), (3) immediately gives the particularly important formula
\[
U_2=u=n^2+2n-4. \tag{5}
\]

We next need a divisibility description of \(U_3\). For \(3\le k\le n\), define
\[
\Sigma_k=\sum_{j=k}^{n-1}(j-3)!,
\]
where an empty sum is zero. We claim that
\[
(k-1)!\,U_k
=(k-2)\left(4(n-1)(n-3)!+u\Sigma_k\right). \tag{6}
\]
Here and below \(0!=1\).

This too follows by downward induction. For \(k=n\), one has \(\Sigma_n=0\) and \(U_n=4\), and (6) reduces to
\[
4(n-1)!=4(n-2)(n-1)(n-3)!,
\]
which is true. Suppose (6) is known at \(k+1\), where \(3\le k<n\). The induction hypothesis says
\[
k!U_{k+1}=(k-1)\left(4(n-1)(n-3)!+u\Sigma_{k+1}\right).
\]
Since
\[
k!=k(k-1)(k-2)(k-3)!,
\]
canceling the nonzero factor \(k-1\) gives
\[
k(k-2)(k-3)!U_{k+1}
=4(n-1)(n-3)!+u\Sigma_{k+1}. \tag{7}
\]
On the other hand, multiply (4) by \((k-2)(k-3)!\). Because
\((k-1)!=(k-1)(k-2)(k-3)!\), this yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
(k-1)!U_k
&=(k-2)(k-3)!\bigl(u+k(k-2)U_{k+1}\bigr)\\
&=(k-2)\left(u(k-3)!+k(k-2)(k-3)!U_{k+1}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using (7) and
\(\Sigma_k=(k-3)!+\Sigma_{k+1}\), we obtain (6).

Set \(k=3\) in (6). Then
\[
2U_3=4(n-1)(n-3)!+u\Sigma_3. \tag{8}
\]
If \(n\ge5\), the integer \(\Sigma_3\) is even. Indeed, its first two terms are
\(0!+1!=2\), while every subsequent term \((j-3)!\), for \(j\ge5\), is divisible by \(2\). Write \(\Sigma_3=2H\). Dividing (8) by \(2\) gives
\[
U_3=uH+2(n-1)(n-3)! \tag{9}
\]
for some integer \(H\).

We now prove the key consequence of these identities. Suppose that
\[
n\ge7,
\]
\(p\) is an odd prime,
\[
p\mid u=n^2+2n-4,
\]
and
\[
n+1\le p. \tag{10}
\]
We claim that \(a(n)=p\).

Write
\[
u=pc.
\]
Since \(u>0\) and \(p>0\), the cofactor \(c\) is a positive integer. From \(p\ge n+1\),
\[
(n+1)c\le pc=u=n^2+2n-4<(n+1)^2,
\]
so \(c<n+1\), hence \(c\le n\). In fact,
\[
c\le n-3. \tag{11}
\]
To see this, we exclude the only three remaining possibilities.

If \(c=n\), then \(n\mid u\). But \(n\mid n^2+2n\), so \(n\mid4\), impossible because \(n\ge7\).

If \(c=n-1\), then \(n-1\mid u\). Reducing \(n\) to \(1\) modulo \(n-1\) gives
\[
u=n^2+2n-4\equiv1+2-4=-1\pmod{n-1}.
\]
Thus \(n-1\mid1\), again impossible for \(n\ge7\).

If \(c=n-2\), then reducing \(n\) to \(2\) modulo \(n-2\) gives
\[
u\equiv 2^2+2\cdot2-4=4\pmod{n-2}.
\]
Thus \(n-2\mid4\), impossible because \(n-2\ge5\). This proves (11).

Every positive integer at most \(n-3\) divides \((n-3)!\), so
\[
c\mid(n-3)!.
\]
Formula (9), together with \(c\mid u\), now shows that
\[
c\mid U_3.
\]
Write
\[
U_3=cd. \tag{12}
\]
Positivity of \(U_3\) and \(c\) implies \(d>0\).

Crucially, \(p\) does not divide \(U_3\). Suppose it did. Since \(p\mid u\), formula (9) would imply
\[
p\mid 2(n-1)(n-3)!.
\]
As \(p\) is prime, it would divide at least one of \(2\), \(n-1\), and \((n-3)!\). It cannot divide \(2\), since it is odd. It cannot divide \(n-1\), since \(0<n-1<p\) by (10). Finally, if a prime divides \((n-3)!\), it divides one of the factors \(1,2,\ldots,n-3\), and therefore is at most \(n-3\), whereas (10) says \(p\ge n+1\). All alternatives are impossible. Hence
\[
p\nmid U_3. \tag{13}
\]
In particular, because \(d\mid U_3\) by (12), one has \(p\nmid d\), so \(p\) and \(d\) are coprime.

Using (2), (5), and (12), we therefore get
\[
R_2(n)=\frac{U_2}{U_3}=\frac{pc}{cd}=\frac pd.
\]
The last fraction is in lowest terms, because \(\gcd(p,d)=1\), and both terms are positive. Consequently
\[
\frac1{R_2(n)}=\frac dp
\]
is also in lowest terms, and its denominator is exactly \(p\). Thus
\[
a(n)=p. \tag{14}
\]

It remains to construct an \(n\) satisfying the hypotheses of this key consequence for each prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\).

First suppose \(p\ge19\). The given congruence implies
\[
p\equiv1\quad\hbox{or}\quad4\pmod5.
\]
Thus \(p\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(5\): the residues \(1\) and \(4\) are respectively \(1^2\) and \(2^2\) modulo \(5\). Since \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), quadratic reciprocity says that, for the distinct odd primes \(5\) and \(p\),
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right).
\]
It follows that \(5\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\). Hence there is an integer \(r\), chosen with
\[
0\le r<p,
\]
such that
\[
r^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{15}
\]
In fact \(r\ne0\), for otherwise (15) would say \(p\mid5\), impossible for \(p\ge19\).

Both \(r\) and \(p-r\) are roots of \(x^2\equiv5\pmod p\). Let
\[
s=\max\{r,p-r\}.
\]
Because \(1\le r\le p-1\), both candidates are at most \(p-1\), so
\[
s\le p-1. \tag{16}
\]
Also \(r+(p-r)=p\), so their maximum is at least \(\lceil p/2\rceil\). Since \(p\ge19\), this gives
\[
s\ge10. \tag{17}
\]
Moreover, whether \(s=r\) or \(s=p-r\), (15) gives
\[
s^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{18}
\]

Now set
\[
n=s-1.
\]
By (17), \(n\ge9\), in particular \(n\ge7\). By (16),
\[
n+1=s\le p-1<p,
\]
so certainly \(n+1\le p\). Finally,
\[
n^2+2n-4=(s-1)^2+2(s-1)-4=s^2-5,
\]
and (18) says that \(p\) divides this integer. All hypotheses used to prove (14) are therefore satisfied, and so \(a(n)=p\).

It remains only to handle primes below \(19\). A positive integer less than \(19\) that is congruent to \(1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) can only be \(1\), \(9\), or \(11\). The first two are not prime, so the only case is \(p=11\). Take \(n=3\). Then the continued fraction has just its final level:
\[
R_2(3)=2-\frac3{-4}=2+\frac34=\frac{11}{4}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac1{R_2(3)}=\frac4{11},
\]
which is reduced, and hence \(a(3)=11\).

Thus every prime congruent to \(1\) or \(9\) modulo \(10\) occurs as a term of A363347.
